title: Reading short authentic texts
blurb: Decode short Czech news snippets and articles by spotting signal words and connectors — your first step toward CCE-style reading tasks.

vocab.example: V článku se uvádí, že cena bytů roste.
V souvislosti s bouřkou byl zrušen let.
V důsledku sněžení byly zavřené školy.
Na konci článku najdete krátké shrnutí.

grammarNote.title: Reading strategy: signal words, not every word
grammarNote.text: Short authentic texts (news snippets, notices, simple articles) don't need to be read word-for-word — spotting a handful of recurring signal words gets you most of the meaning fast. "Podle" flags where a claim comes from (podle zprávy, podle ministerstva). "Uvádí se, že..." and "tvrdí se, že..." are the impersonal reflexive constructions Czech journalism uses instead of naming a speaker directly — treat them as "it is reported/claimed that...". Cause-and-effect connectors are worth memorizing as fixed chunks with their case: "v souvislosti s" takes the instrumental (s bouřkou), "v důsledku" takes the genitive (sněžení), and "dochází k" takes the dative (k nehodám) — the preposition, not the verb, tells you which case to expect. Once you can recognize these, you can skim past unfamiliar vocabulary and still follow the structure: source → claim → cause → result.

check.prompt: Which phrase typically introduces the source of information in a news text?
check.explanation: "Podle" ("according to") signals where a claim in the text comes from, e.g. podle zprávy, podle ministerstva.
check.note: Learning to spot source markers like this lets you separate reported facts from the article's own claims.

check.prompt: "V souvislosti s" (in connection with) is followed by the instrumental case.
check.explanation: Correct — s always takes the instrumental, so v souvislosti s bouřkou ("in connection with the storm") uses bouřkou, the instrumental of bouřka.

check.prompt: Na křižovatce dochází k ___. (nehoda — accidents, dative plural)
check.explanation: "Dochází k" always takes the dative — nehoda becomes nehodám in the dative plural.

check.prompt: Rewrite as a reported claim using "uvádí se, že": "Ceny bytů rostou." → ___
accepted: Uvádí se, že ceny bytů rostou.
V článku se uvádí, že ceny bytů rostou.
check.explanation: "Uvádí se, že..." is the standard impersonal way Czech news texts report a claim without naming who said it.

title: Listening to natural speech
blurb: Tune your ear to real spoken Czech — interview fillers, colloquial shortcuts, and the fixed phrases used in public announcements.

vocab.example: Vážení cestující, vlak má zpoždění deset minut.
Vlak nejede z důvodu opravy trati.
Omlouváme se za zpoždění způsobené počasím.

grammarNote.title: Real speech is faster and looser than lesson audio
grammarNote.text: Two things trip learners up when they first listen to authentic Czech. First, casual conversation runs on filler words that carry almost no literal meaning — vlastně, prostě, jakoby, no jasně — they buy the speaker thinking time and signal attitude, not content, so don't stop to translate them word-for-word. Casual spoken Czech (obecná čeština) also shortens and merges sounds compared to the "correct" written form you learn from textbooks: já jsem often becomes já sem, and adjective endings like -ý slide toward -ej (mladý → mladej) in relaxed speech. Second, public announcements (trains, planes, stores) use a small set of fixed formal phrases that recur identically everywhere, so they're worth memorizing as whole chunks rather than decoding on the fly: Vážení cestující (dear passengers), Upozorňujeme, že... (please note that...), z důvodu + genitive (due to...), and Omlouváme se za... (we apologize for...).

check.prompt: Which of these is a fixed formal announcement phrase, not a casual filler word?
check.explanation: "Z důvodu" ("due to") is part of the fixed formal register used in announcements, unlike the casual fillers vlastně, jakoby, and prostě.

check.prompt: Colloquial spoken Czech (obecná čeština) always matches written/standard Czech (spisovná čeština) exactly.
check.explanation: False — casual speech regularly shortens sounds and changes endings (e.g. mladý → mladej) compared to the standard written form.
"Z důvodu" + genitive is the standard formal way to state a cause in announcements.

check.prompt: Vlak nejede z důvodu opravy trati. → Change the reason to bouřka (storm): ___
check.explanation: "Z důvodu" takes the genitive — bouřka becomes bouřky in the genitive.

title: Formal vs. informal register
blurb: Know when to switch from ty to Vy, and how formal Czech letters and emails differ from everyday speech.

vocab.example: Dobrý den, jmenuji se Jana Nováková.

vocab.translation: I would like to ask you for... (formal)
vocab.example: Prosím Vás o odpověď co nejdříve.
Vážený pane Nováku, děkuji za Váš e-mail.

grammarNote.title: Ty vs. Vy — and capitalizing Vy in writing
grammarNote.text: Czech marks formality directly through the pronoun you use: ty for family, friends, children, and peers your own age; vy for strangers, official contexts, and anyone clearly senior to you at work — the same tu/vous split as French or German. Switching from vy to ty with someone is treated as a small social event, usually marked by asking Budeme si tykat? ("shall we use ty with each other?"). In formal written Czech — letters, emails, official forms — the formal Vy, Váš, and Vám are capitalized as a mark of respect, even though vy is never capitalized in formal spoken Czech. Formal letters and emails also follow a fixed shape: open with Vážený pane / Vážená paní + surname, keep the body free of contractions and slang, and close with S pozdravem followed by your full name — this exact structure is what the B2 Writing subtest expects for formal letters.

check.prompt: In a formal written letter or email, how is the formal "you" written?
check.explanation: Formal Vy/Váš/Vám are capitalized in formal writing as a sign of respect, even though this capitalization doesn't apply in speech.

check.prompt: Ty is an appropriate way to address a stranger in a formal business email.
check.explanation: False — a stranger or business contact should be addressed with the formal Vy, not ty.

check.prompt: Vážený pane Nováku, děkuji za ___ e-mail. (your — formal, capitalized)
check.explanation: Formal Váš is capitalized in written Czech, unlike the informal tvůj.

check.prompt: Rewrite informally as a formal greeting: "Ahoj, jak se máš?" → ___
check.explanation: The formal greeting Dobrý den pairs with the formal verb form máte (vy-form), replacing the informal Ahoj and máš.
